During the last 18 years of his life, he gave away around $350 million (equivalent to $6.9 billion in 2025 dollars), almost 90 percent of his fortune, to charities, foundations and universities.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-ACLegacy-6) His 1889 article proclaiming "[The Gospel of Wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel_of_Wealth "The Gospel of Wealth") " called on the rich to use their wealth to improve society, expressed support for [progressive taxation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_tax "Progressive tax") and an [estate tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inheritance_tax "Inheritance tax") , and stimulated a wave of philanthropy. Carnegie was born in [Dunfermline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunfermline "Dunfermline") , Scotland. He immigrated to what is now [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh") , Pennsylvania, with his parents in 1848 at the age of 12. Carnegie started work in a cotton mill and later worked as a [telegrapher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegrapher "Telegrapher") . By the 1860s, he had investments in railroads, railroad sleeping cars, bridges, and oil [derricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derrick "Derrick") . He accumulated further wealth as a bond salesman, raising money for American enterprise in Europe. He built Pittsburgh's [Carnegie Steel Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company") , which he sold to [J. P. Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Morgan "J. P. Morgan") in 1901 for $303,450,000;[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Hawke_1980-7) it formed the basis of the [U.S. Steel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel "U.S. Steel") . After selling Carnegie Steel, he surpassed [John D. Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller "John D. Rockefeller") as the richest American of the time.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-8) Carnegie devoted the remainder of his life to large-scale philanthropy, with special emphasis on [building local libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_library "Carnegie library") , working for world peace, education, and scientific research. He funded [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") in New York City, the [Peace Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Palace "Peace Palace") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") , founded the [Carnegie Corporation of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Corporation_of_New_York "Carnegie Corporation of New York") , [Carnegie Endowment for International Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Endowment_for_International_Peace "Carnegie Endowment for International Peace") , [Carnegie Institution for Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Institution_for_Science "Carnegie Institution for Science") , [Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Trust_for_the_Universities_of_Scotland "Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland") , [Carnegie Hero Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hero_Fund "Carnegie Hero Fund") , [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") , and the [Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museums_of_Pittsburgh "Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh") , among others. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Birthplace_of_Andrew_Carnegie%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/500px-Birthplace_of_Andrew_Carnegie%2C_Dunfermline.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birthplace_of_Andrew_Carnegie,_Dunfermline.jpg) Birthplace of Andrew Carnegie in [Dunfermline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunfermline "Dunfermline") , Scotland Andrew Carnegie was born to William Carnegie and Margaret (Morrison) Carnegie in Dunfermline, Scotland,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-:1-9) in a typical weaver's cottage with only one main room. It consisted of half the ground floor, which was shared with the neighboring weaver's family.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-MacKay_pp23-24-10) The main room served as a living room, dining room and bedroom.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-MacKay_pp23-24-10) He was named after his paternal grandfather.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-MacKay_pp23-24-10) William Carnegie had a successful weaving business and owned multiple looms.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-:1-9) In 1836, the family moved to a larger house in Edgar Street (opposite Reid's Park), following the demand for more heavy [damask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damask "Damask") , from which his father benefited.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-MacKay_pp23-24-10) Carnegie was educated at the Free School in Dunfermline, a gift to the town from philanthropist [Adam Rolland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Rolland "Adam Rolland") of Gask.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-11) Carnegie's maternal uncle, Scottish political leader [George Lauder Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lauder_Sr. "George Lauder Sr.") , deeply influenced him as a boy by introducing him to [Robert Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burns "Robert Burns") ' writings[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdge20044-12) and historical Scottish heroes such as [Robert the Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_the_Bruce "Robert the Bruce") , [William Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wallace "William Wallace") , and [Rob Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Roy_MacGregor "Rob Roy MacGregor") . Lauder's son, also named [George Lauder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lauder_(industrialist) "George Lauder (industrialist)") , grew up with Carnegie and later became his business partner in the United States.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-13) When Carnegie was 12, his father had fallen on tough times as a handloom weaver. Making matters worse, the country was in starvation. His mother helped support the family by assisting her brother and by selling potted meats at her "sweetie shop", becoming the primary breadwinner.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Nasaw-14) Struggling to make ends meet, the Carnegies borrowed money from George Lauder, Sr.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-15) and moved to the United States in 1848 for the prospect of a better life. They headed to [Allegheny, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania") , where they heard there was a demand for workers.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-MacKay_pp37-38-16) Carnegie's emigration to America was his second journey outside Dunfermline. The first was a family outing to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") to see [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria") .[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-17) In September 1848, Carnegie and his family arrived in Allegheny. Carnegie's father struggled to sell his product on his own.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-18) Eventually, the father and son both received job offers at Anchor Cotton Mills, a Scottish-owned facility. Carnegie's first job in 1848 was as a [bobbin boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobbin_boy "Bobbin boy") , changing spools of thread in a cotton mill 12 hours a day, 6 days a week in a Pittsburgh cotton factory. His starting wage was $1.20 per week (equivalent to $45 in 2025[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-inflation-US-19) ).[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-20) His father soon quit his position at the cotton mill, returning to his loom, and was again removed as a substantial breadwinner.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-:0-21) But Carnegie attracted the attention of John Hay, a Scottish manufacturer of bobbins, who offered him a job for $2.00 per week (equivalent to $74 in 2025[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-inflation-US-19) ).[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-22) In his autobiography, Carnegie writes about the hardships he had to endure with this new job: > Soon after this Mr. John Hay, a fellow Scotch manufacturer of bobbins in Allegheny City, needed a boy, and asked whether I would not go into his service. I went, and received two dollars per week; but at first the work was even more irksome than the factory. I had to run a small steam-engine and to fire the boiler in the cellar of the bobbin factory. It was too much for me. I found myself night after night, sitting up in bed trying the steam gauges, fearing at one time that the steam was too low and that the workers above would complain that they had not power enough, and at another time that the steam was too high and that the boiler might burst.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-23) ### Telegraph [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Andrew_and_Thomas_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg/500px-Andrew_and_Thomas_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_and_Thomas_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg) Carnegie, age 16, with younger brother Thomas, c. 1851 In 1849,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-24) Carnegie became a telegraph messenger boy in the Pittsburgh Office of the Ohio Telegraph Company,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-25) following the recommendation of his uncle. He was a hard worker and would memorize all of the locations of Pittsburgh's businesses and the faces of important men. He made many connections this way. He also paid close attention to his work and quickly learned to distinguish the different sounds the incoming telegraph signals produced. He developed the ability to translate signals by ear, without using the paper slip.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-26) Within a year he was promoted to an operator. Carnegie's education and passion for reading were given a boost by [Colonel James Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Byers_Anderson "John Byers Anderson") , who opened his personal library of 400 volumes to working boys each Saturday night.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-27) Carnegie was a consistent borrower and a "[self-made man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-made_man "Self-made man") " in both his economic development and his intellectual and cultural development. He was so grateful to Colonel Anderson for the use of his library that he "resolved, if ever wealth came to me, \[to see to it\] that other poor boys might receive opportunities similar to those for which we were indebted to the nobleman".[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-28) ### Railroads Starting in 1853, when Carnegie was around 18 years old, [Thomas A. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_A._Scott "Thomas A. Scott") of the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad") employed him as a secretary/telegraph operator at a salary of $4.00 per week ($155 by 2025). Carnegie accepted the job with the railroad as he saw more prospects for career growth and experience there than with the telegraph company.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Nasaw-14) When Carnegie was 24 years old, Scott asked him if he could handle being superintendent of the Western Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Edge_2004_pg._35-29) On December 1, 1859, Carnegie officially became superintendent of the Western Division. He hired his sixteen-year-old brother Tom to be his personal secretary and telegraph operator. Carnegie also hired his cousin, Maria Hogan, who became the first female telegraph operator in the country.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-30) As superintendent, Carnegie made a salary of $1500 a year ($54,000 by 2025 inflation).[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Edge_2004_pg._35-29) His employment by the Pennsylvania Railroad would be vital to his later success. The railroads were the first big businesses in America, and the Pennsylvania was one of the largest. Carnegie learned much about management and cost control during these years, and from Scott in particular.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Nasaw-14) Scott also helped him with his first investments. Many of these were part of the corruption indulged in by Scott and the president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, [John Edgar Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edgar_Thomson "John Edgar Thomson") , which consisted of inside trading in companies with which the railroad did business, or payoffs made by contracting parties "as part of a _[quid pro quo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quid_pro_quo "Quid pro quo") _".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Nasaw_pg59_60-31) In 1855, Scott made it possible for Carnegie to invest $500 in the [Adams Express Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_Express_Company "Adams Express Company") , which contracted with the Pennsylvania to carry its messengers. The money was secured by his mother's placing of a $600 mortgage on the family's $700 home, but the opportunity was available only because of Carnegie's close relationship with Scott.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Nasaw_pg59_60-31) [\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-32) A few years later, he received a few shares in [Theodore Tuttle Woodruff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Tuttle_Woodruff "Theodore Tuttle Woodruff") 's sleeping car company as a reward for holding shares that Woodruff had given to Scott and Thomson, as a payoff. Reinvesting his returns in such inside investments in railroad-related industries (iron, bridges, and [rails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_(rail_transport) "Track (rail transport)") ), Carnegie slowly accumulated capital, the basis for his later success. Throughout his later career, he made use of his close connections to Thomson and Scott, as he established businesses that supplied rails and bridges to the railroad, offering the two men stakes in his enterprises. ### 1860–1865: American Civil War [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Pullman_sleeping_car_circa_1860s.JPG/960px-Pullman_sleeping_car_circa_1860s.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pullman_sleeping_car_circa_1860s.JPG) Pullman sleeping car, where Carnegie made one of his most successful investments Before the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") , Carnegie arranged a merger between Woodruff's company and that of [George Pullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pullman "George Pullman") , the inventor of the [sleeping car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_(car_or_coach) "Pullman (car or coach)") for [first-class travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_class_travel "First class travel") , which facilitated business travel at distances over 500 miles (800 km). The investment proved a success and a source of profit for Woodruff and Carnegie. The young Carnegie continued to work for Pennsylvania's Tom Scott and introduced several improvements in the service.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-EB1911-33) In the spring of 1861, Carnegie joined the [U.S. Military Telegraph Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Military_Telegraph_Corps "U.S. Military Telegraph Corps") and was appointed by Scott, who was now Assistant Secretary of War in charge of military transportation, as Superintendent of the Military Railways and the Union Government's telegraph lines in the East. Carnegie helped open the rail lines into Washington, D.C. that the rebels had cut; he rode the locomotive pulling the first brigade of Union troops to reach Washington, D.C. Following the defeat of Union forces at [Bull Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Bull_Run "First Battle of Bull Run") , he personally supervised the transportation of the defeated forces. Under his organization, the telegraph service rendered efficient service to the Union cause and significantly assisted in the eventual victory. Carnegie later joked that he was "the first casualty of the war" when he gained a scar on his cheek from freeing a trapped telegraph wire.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-34) The defeat of the Confederacy required vast supplies of [munitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munition "Munition") , with railroads and telegraph lines being required to deliver them efficiently. The war demonstrated how integral the industries were to Union success.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-35) ### Keystone Bridge Company [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Eads_Bridge_from_Laclede%27s_Landing%2C_Sep_2012.jpg/960px-Eads_Bridge_from_Laclede%27s_Landing%2C_Sep_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eads_Bridge_from_Laclede's_Landing,_Sep_2012.jpg) Eads Bridge across the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") , opened in 1874 using Carnegie steel In 1864, Carnegie was one of the early investors in the Columbia Oil Company in [Venango County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venango_County,_Pennsylvania "Venango County, Pennsylvania") .[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-36) In one year, the firm yielded over $1 million in cash dividends, and petroleum from oil wells on the property sold profitably. The demand for iron products, such as armor for gunboats, cannons, and shells, as well as a hundred other industrial products, made Pittsburgh a center of wartime production. Carnegie worked with others in establishing a steel [rolling mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_mill "Rolling mill") , and steel production and control of industry became the source of his fortune. Carnegie had some investments in the iron industry before the war. After the war, Carnegie left the railroads to devote his energies to the ironworks trade. Carnegie worked to develop several ironworks, eventually forming the Keystone Bridge Works and the Union Ironworks, in Pittsburgh. Although he had left the Pennsylvania Railroad Company, he remained connected to its management, namely Thomas A. Scott and J. Edgar Thomson. He used his connection to the two men to acquire contracts for his [Keystone Bridge Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_Bridge_Company "Keystone Bridge Company") and the rails produced by his [ironworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworks "Ironworks") . He also gave stock in his businesses to Scott and Thomson, and the Pennsylvania was his best customer. When he built his first steel plant, he made a point of naming it after Thomson. As well as having good business sense, Carnegie possessed charm and literary knowledge. He was invited to many important social functions, which Carnegie exploited to his advantage.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-37) Carnegie, through Keystone, supplied the steel for and owned shares in the landmark [Eads Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge") project across the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") at [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") , Missouri (completed 1874). This project was an important proof-of-concept for steel technology, which marked the opening of a new steel market. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Andrew_Carnegie_circa_1878_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg/500px-Andrew_Carnegie_circa_1878_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Carnegie_circa_1878_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg) Carnegie, c. 1878 Carnegie believed in using his fortune for others and doing more than making money. In 1868, at age 33, he wrote:[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-38) [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-39) > I propose to take an income no greater than $50,000 per annum! Beyond this I need ever earn, make no effort to increase my fortune, but spend the surplus each year for benevolent purposes! Let us cast aside business forever, except for others. Let us settle in Oxford and I shall get a thorough education, making the acquaintance of literary men. I figure that this will take three years' active work. I shall pay especial attention to speaking in public. We can settle in London and I can purchase a controlling interest in some newspaper or live review and give the general management of it attention, taking part in public matters, especially those connected with education and improvement of the poorer classes. Man must have no idol and the amassing of wealth is one of the worst species of [idolatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idolatry "Idolatry") > ! No idol is more debasing than the worship of money! Whatever I engage in I must push inordinately; therefore should I be careful to choose that life which will be the most elevating in its character. To continue much longer overwhelmed by business cares and with most of my thoughts wholly upon the way to make more money in the shortest time, must degrade me beyond hope of permanent recovery. I will resign business at thirty-five, but during these ensuing two years I wish to spend the afternoons in receiving instruction and in reading systematically! ### Industrialist #### 1875–1900: Steel empire [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/61/Bessemer_converter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bessemer_converter.jpg) Bessemer converter [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/US-PA%281891%29_p750_BESSEMER%2C_THE_EDGAR_THOMSON_STEEL_WORKS_AND_BLAST-FURNACES.jpg/960px-US-PA%281891%29_p750_BESSEMER%2C_THE_EDGAR_THOMSON_STEEL_WORKS_AND_BLAST-FURNACES.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US-PA(1891)_p750_BESSEMER,_THE_EDGAR_THOMSON_STEEL_WORKS_AND_BLAST-FURNACES.jpg) The Edgar Thomson Steel Works and Blast-Furnaces in Braddock, Pennsylvania (1891) Carnegie made his fortune in the steel industry, controlling the most extensive integrated iron and steel operations ever owned by an individual in the United States. One of his two great innovations was in the cheap and efficient mass production of steel by adopting and adapting the [Bessemer process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessemer_process "Bessemer process") , which allowed the high carbon content of [pig iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig_iron "Pig iron") to be burnt away in a controlled and rapid way during [steel production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_production "Steel production") . Steel prices dropped as a result, and Bessemer steel was rapidly adopted for rails; however, it was not suitable for buildings and bridges.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-40) The second was in his [vertical integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_integration "Vertical integration") of all suppliers of raw materials. In 1883, Carnegie bought the rival [Homestead Steel Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Steel_Works "Homestead Steel Works") , which included an extensive plant served by tributary coal and iron fields, a 425-mile-long (684 km) railway, and a line of [lake steamships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_freighter "Lake freighter") .[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-EB1911-33) In the late 1880s, Carnegie Steel was the largest manufacturer of pig iron, steel rails, and [coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_(fuel) "Coke (fuel)") in the world, with a capacity to produce approximately 2,000 tons of pig iron per day. By 1889, the U.S. output of steel exceeded that of the UK, and Carnegie owned a large part of it. Carnegie's empire grew to include the [J. Edgar Thomson Steel Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thomson_Steel_Works "Edgar Thomson Steel Works") in [Braddock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braddock,_Pennsylvania "Braddock, Pennsylvania") , Pennsylvania (named for [John Edgar Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edgar_Thomson "John Edgar Thomson") , Carnegie's former boss and president of the Pennsylvania Railroad), the Pittsburgh Bessemer Steel Works, the [Lucy Furnaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Furnace "Lucy Furnace") , the Union Iron Mills, the Union Mill (Wilson, Walker & County), the Keystone Bridge Works, the Hartman Steel Works, the Frick Coke Company, and the [Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotia,_Pennsylvania "Scotia, Pennsylvania") , Pennsylvania ore mines. Carnegie combined his assets and those of his associates in 1892 with the launching of the [Carnegie Steel Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company") .[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-41) Carnegie's success was also due to his relationship with the railroad industries, which not only relied on steel for track, but were also making money from steel transport. The steel and railroad barons worked closely to negotiate prices instead of allowing free-market competition.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-42) Besides Carnegie's market manipulation, United States trade tariffs were also working in favor of the steel industry. Carnegie spent energy and resources lobbying Congress for a continuation of favorable tariffs from which he earned millions of dollars a year.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-43) Carnegie tried to keep this information concealed, but legal documents released in 1900, during proceedings with the ex-chairman of Carnegie Steel, [Henry Clay Frick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay_Frick "Henry Clay Frick") , revealed how favorable the tariffs had been.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-44) While owning steel works, Carnegie had purchased at low cost the most valuable of the iron ore fields around [Lake Superior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior "Lake Superior") . #### 1901: U.S. Steel In 1901, Carnegie was 65 years of age and considering retirement. He reformed his enterprises into conventional [joint stock corporations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") as preparation for this. [John Pierpont Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Morgan "J. P. Morgan") was a banker and America's most important financial deal maker. He had observed how efficiently Carnegie produced profits. He envisioned an integrated steel industry that would cut costs, lower prices to consumers, produce in greater quantities and raise wages to workers. To this end, he needed to buy out Carnegie and several other major producers and integrate them into one company, thereby eliminating duplication and waste. He concluded negotiations on March 2, 1901, and formed the [United States Steel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel "U.S. Steel") . It was the first corporation in the world with a market capitalization of over $1 billion. The buyout, secretly negotiated by [Charles M. Schwab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_M._Schwab "Charles M. Schwab") (no relation to [Charles R. Schwab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_R._Schwab "Charles R. Schwab") ), was the largest such industrial takeover in United States history to date. The holdings were incorporated in the United States Steel Corporation, a trust organized by Morgan, and Carnegie retired from business.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-EB1911-33) His steel enterprises were bought out for $303,450,000.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Hawke_1980-7) Carnegie's share of this amounted to $225.64 million (in 2025, $8.73 billion), which was paid to him in the form of 5%, 50-year gold bonds. The letter agreeing to sell his share was signed on February 26, 1901. On March 2, the circular formally filed the organization and capitalization (at $1.4 billion—4% of the U.S. gross domestic product at the time) of the United States Steel Corporation actually completed the contract. The bonds were to be delivered within two weeks to the Hudson Trust Company of [Hoboken, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_New_Jersey "Hoboken, New Jersey") , in trust to Robert A. Franks, Carnegie's business secretary. There, a special vault was built to house the physical bulk of nearly $230 million worth of bonds.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-45) ### Scholar and activist #### 1880–1900 Carnegie continued his business career; some of his literary intentions were fulfilled. He befriended the English poet [Matthew Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Arnold "Matthew Arnold") , the English philosopher [Herbert Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Spencer "Herbert Spencer") , and the American humorist [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain "Mark Twain") , as well as being in correspondence and acquaintance with most of the [U.S. Presidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") ,[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinkler2006172-46) statesmen, and notable writers.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinkler200613-47) Carnegie constructed commodious [swimming-baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_baths "Swimming baths") for the people of his hometown in [Dunfermline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunfermline "Dunfermline") in 1879. In the following year, Carnegie gave £8,000 for the establishment of a [Dunfermline Carnegie Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunfermline_Carnegie_Library "Dunfermline Carnegie Library") in Scotland. In 1884, he gave $50,000 to [Bellevue Hospital Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hospital_Medical_College "Bellevue Hospital Medical College") (now part of [New York University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYU_Langone_Medical_Center "NYU Langone Medical Center") ) to create a [histological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histology "Histology") laboratory, now called the Carnegie Laboratory. In 1881, Carnegie took his family, including his 70-year-old mother, on a trip to the United Kingdom. They toured Scotland by coach and enjoyed several receptions en route. The highlight was a return to Dunfermline, where Carnegie's mother laid the foundation stone of a [Carnegie Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Library "Carnegie Library") which he funded. Carnegie's criticism of British society did not mean dislike; on the contrary, one of Carnegie's ambitions was to act as a [catalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalyst "Catalyst") for a close association between English-speaking peoples. To this end, in the early 1880s in partnership with [Samuel Storey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Storey_(Liberal_politician) "Samuel Storey (Liberal politician)") , he purchased numerous newspapers in Britain, all of which were to advocate the abolition of the monarchy and the establishment of "the British Republic". Carnegie's charm, aided by his wealth, afforded him many British friends, including Prime Minister [William Ewart Gladstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ewart_Gladstone "William Ewart Gladstone") . In 1886, Carnegie's younger brother Thomas died at age 43. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/James_Bryce%2C_1st_Viscount_Bryce_%26_Andrew_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg/500px-James_Bryce%2C_1st_Viscount_Bryce_%26_Andrew_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Bryce,_1st_Viscount_Bryce_&_Andrew_Carnegie_-_Project_Gutenberg_eText_17976.jpg) Carnegie, right, with [James Bryce, 1st Viscount Bryce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bryce,_1st_Viscount_Bryce "James Bryce, 1st Viscount Bryce") Following his tour of the UK, he wrote about his experiences in a book entitled _An American Four-in-hand in Britain_. In 1886, Carnegie wrote his most radical work to date, entitled _Triumphant Democracy_. Liberal in its use of statistics to make its arguments, the book argued his view that the American republican system of government was superior to the British [monarchical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy "Monarchy") system. It gave a highly favorable and idealized view of American progress and criticized the British royal family. The cover depicted an upended royal [crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown "Crown") and a broken scepter. The book created considerable controversy in the UK. The book made many Americans appreciate their country's economic progress and sold over 40,000 copies, mostly in the U.S. Although actively involved in running his many businesses, Carnegie had become a regular contributor to numerous magazines, most notably _[The Nineteenth Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteenth_Century_(periodical) "Nineteenth Century (periodical)") _, under the editorship of [James Knowles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thomas_Knowles_(1831%E2%80%931908) "James Thomas Knowles (1831–1908)") , and the influential _North American Review_, led by the editor [Lloyd Bryce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Bryce "Lloyd Bryce") . In 1889, Carnegie published "Wealth" in the June issue of the _North American Review_.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-48) After reading it, Gladstone requested its publication in Britain, where it appeared as "The Gospel of Wealth" in _[The Pall Mall Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pall_Mall_Gazette "The Pall Mall Gazette") _. Carnegie argued that the life of a wealthy industrialist should comprise two parts. The first part was the gathering and the accumulation of wealth. The second part was for the subsequent distribution of this wealth to benevolent causes. Philanthropy was key to making life worthwhile. Carnegie was a well-regarded writer. He published three books on travel.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-49) ### Anti-imperialism In the aftermath of the [Spanish–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War "Spanish–American War") , the United States seemed poised to annex [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Cuba_(1902%E2%80%931959) "Republic of Cuba (1902–1959)") , [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam") , [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") and the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insular_Government_of_the_Philippine_Islands "Insular Government of the Philippine Islands") . Carnegie strongly opposed the idea of American colonies. He opposed the annexation of the Philippines almost to the point of supporting [William Jennings Bryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan "William Jennings Bryan") against McKinley in 1900. In 1898, Carnegie tried to arrange independence for the Philippines. As the conclusion of the Spanish–American War neared, the United States purchased the Philippines from Spain for $20 million. To counter what he perceived as [American imperialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_imperialism "American imperialism") , Carnegie personally offered $20 million to the Philippines so that the [Filipino people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipinos "Filipinos") could purchase their independence from the United States.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-50) However, nothing came of the offer. In 1898 Carnegie joined the [American Anti-Imperialist League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Anti-Imperialist_League "American Anti-Imperialist League") , in opposition to the U.S. annexation of the Philippines. Andrew Carnegie's philanthropy. _Puck_ magazine cartoon by Louis Dalrymple, 1903 Carnegie spent his last years as a philanthropist. From 1901 forward, public attention was turned from the shrewd business acumen which had enabled Carnegie to accumulate such a fortune, to the public-spirited way in which he devoted himself to using it on philanthropic projects. He had written about his views on social subjects and the responsibilities of great wealth in _Triumphant Democracy_ (1886) and [_Gospel of Wealth_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel_of_Wealth "The Gospel of Wealth") (1889). Carnegie devoted the rest of his life to providing capital for purposes of public interest and social and educational advancement. He saved letters of appreciation from those he helped in a desk drawer labeled "Gratitude and Sweet Words." He provided $25,000 a year to the movement for [spelling reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spelling_reform "Spelling reform") .[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-53) His organization, the [Simplified Spelling Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Spelling_Board "Simplified Spelling Board") ,[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-NYT19060306-54) created the _Handbook of Simplified Spelling_, which was written wholly in reformed spelling.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-55) [\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-56) #### 3,000 public libraries [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Andrew_Carnegie%2C_Vanity_Fair%2C_1903-10-29.jpg/500px-Andrew_Carnegie%2C_Vanity_Fair%2C_1903-10-29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Carnegie,_Vanity_Fair,_1903-10-29.jpg) Captioned "Free Libraries", Carnegie caricatured by "[Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Ward "Leslie Ward") " for the London magazine _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity_Fair_(British_magazine) "Vanity Fair (British magazine)") _, 1903 Among his many philanthropic efforts, the establishment of [public libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_library "Public library") throughout the United States, Britain, Canada, New Zealand, and mostly other English-speaking countries was especially prominent. In this special driving interest of his, Carnegie was inspired by meetings with philanthropist [Enoch Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enoch_Pratt "Enoch Pratt") (1808–1896). The [Enoch Pratt Free Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enoch_Pratt_Free_Library "Enoch Pratt Free Library") (1886) of [Baltimore, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore,_Maryland "Baltimore, Maryland") , impressed Carnegie deeply; he said, "Pratt was my guide and inspiration."[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-57) Carnegie turned over management of the library project by 1908 to his staff, led by [James Bertram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bertram_(Carnegie_secretary) "James Bertram (Carnegie secretary)") (1874–1934).[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-58) The first [Carnegie Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Library "Carnegie Library") opened in 1883 in Dunfermline. His method was to provide funds to build and equip the library, but only on the condition that the local authority matched that by providing the land and a budget for operation and maintenance.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-59) To secure local interest, in 1885, he gave $500,000 to [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh") , Pennsylvania, for a public library; in 1886, he gave $250,000 to [Allegheny City, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_City,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny City, Pennsylvania") , for a music hall and library; and he gave $250,000 to [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") , Scotland, for a free library. In total, Carnegie funded some 3,000 libraries, located in 47 U.S. states, and also in Canada, Britain, Ireland, Belgium, Serbia, France, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") , and [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji "Fiji") . He also donated £50,000 to help set up the [University of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham "University of Birmingham") in 1899.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-60) As Van Slyck (1991) showed, during the last years of the 19th century, there was the increasing adoption of the idea that free libraries should be available to the American public. But the design of such libraries was the subject of prolonged and heated debate. On one hand, the library profession called for designs that supported efficiency in administration and operation; on the other, wealthy philanthropists favored buildings that reinforced the paternalistic metaphor and enhanced civic pride. Between 1886 and 1917, Carnegie reformed both library philanthropy and library design, encouraging a closer correspondence between the two.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-61) Carnegie's libraries also served as institutions of control. The telescope saw [first light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_light_(astronomy) "First light (astronomy)") on November 2, 1917, with Carnegie still alive.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-64) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Pittencrieff_Park%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/500px-Pittencrieff_Park%2C_Dunfermline.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pittencrieff_Park,_Dunfermline.jpg) Pittencrieff Park, [Dunfermline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunfermline "Dunfermline") , Scotland In 1901, in Scotland, he gave $10 million to establish the [Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Trust_for_the_Universities_of_Scotland "Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland") . The establishing gift of $10 million was then an unprecedented sum: at the time, total government assistance to all four Scottish universities was about £50,000 a year. The aim of the Trust was to improve and extend the opportunities for scientific research in the Scottish universities and to enable the deserving and qualified youth of Scotland to attend a university.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-65) He was subsequently elected [Lord Rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Rector "Lord Rector") of [University of St. Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St._Andrews "University of St. Andrews") in December 1901,[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-66) and formally installed as such in October 1902,[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-67) serving until 1907. A statue of Carnegie was later built between 1913 and 1914 in the park as a commemoration for his creation of the park.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-69) [\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-70) [\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-71) Carnegie was a major patron of music. His interest in music led him to fund the construction of 7,000 pipe organs in churches and temples, with no apparent preference for any religious denomination or sect.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-73) [\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-74) He gave a further $10 million in 1913 to endow the [Carnegie United Kingdom Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_United_Kingdom_Trust "Carnegie United Kingdom Trust") , a grant-making foundation.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-75) [\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-76) He transferred to the trust the charge of all his existing and future benefactions, other than university benefactions in the United Kingdom. The fraternity's mission reflects Carnegie's values by developing young men to share their talents to create harmony in the world. ### Death [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Andrew_Carnegie_Gravesite.JPG/960px-Andrew_Carnegie_Gravesite.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Andrew_Carnegie_Gravesite.JPG) [Andrew Carnegie's gravestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#Andrew_Carnegie_gravestone "Sleepy Hollow Cemetery") at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in [Sleepy Hollow, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow,_New_York "Sleepy Hollow, New York") Carnegie died on August 11, 1919, in [Lenox, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenox,_Massachusetts "Lenox, Massachusetts") , at his [Shadow Brook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Brook_Farm_Historic_District "Shadow Brook Farm Historic District") estate, of [bronchial pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronchial_pneumonia "Bronchial pneumonia") .[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-81) [\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Krass-82) He had already given away $350,695,653 (approximately $6.9 billion in 2025 dollars) of his wealth. Carnegie is buried only a few yards away from union organizer [Samuel Gompers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Gompers "Samuel Gompers") , another important figure of industry in the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age") .[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-84) Controversies ------------- ### 1889: Johnstown Flood Main article: [Johnstown Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnstown_Flood "Johnstown Flood") [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/The_Great_Conemaugh_Valley_Disaster.jpg/960px-The_Great_Conemaugh_Valley_Disaster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Great_Conemaugh_Valley_Disaster.jpg) A contemporary rendition of the Johnstown Flood scene at the Stone Bridge by [Kurz and Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurz_and_Allison "Kurz and Allison") (1890) Carnegie was one of more than 50 members of the [South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Fork_Fishing_and_Hunting_Club "South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club") , which has been blamed for the [Johnstown Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnstown_Flood "Johnstown Flood") that killed 2,209 people in 1889.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-85) At the suggestion of his friend Benjamin Ruff, Carnegie's partner [Henry Clay Frick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay_Frick "Henry Clay Frick") had formed the exclusive South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club high above Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The sixty-odd club members were the leading business tycoons of Western Pennsylvania and included among their number Frick's best friend, [Andrew Mellon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_W._Mellon "Andrew W. Mellon") , his attorneys [Philander Knox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philander_Knox "Philander Knox") and James Hay Reed, as well as Frick's business partner, Carnegie. High above the city, near the small town of South Fork, the [South Fork Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Fork_Dam "South Fork Dam") was originally built between 1838 and 1853 by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania as part of a canal system to be used as a reservoir for a canal basin in Johnstown. With the coming-of-age of railroads superseding canal barge transport, the lake was abandoned by the Commonwealth, sold to the Pennsylvania Railroad, and sold again to private interests, and eventually came to be owned by the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club in 1881. Prior to the flood, speculators had purchased the abandoned reservoir, made less than well-engineered repairs to the old dam, raised the lake level, built cottages and a clubhouse, and created the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club. Less than 20 miles (32 km) downstream from the dam sat the city of Johnstown. The dam was 72 feet (22 m) high and 931 feet (284 m) long. Between 1881, when the club was opened, and 1889, the dam frequently sprang leaks and was patched, mostly with mud and straw. Additionally, a previous owner removed and sold for scrap the three [cast iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_iron "Cast iron") discharge pipes that previously allowed a controlled release of water. There had been some speculation as to the dam's integrity, and concerns had been raised by the head of the Cambria Iron Works downstream in Johnstown. Such repair work, a reduction in height, and unusually high snowmelt and heavy spring rains combined to cause the dam to give way on May 31, 1889, resulting in twenty million tons of water sweeping down the valley as the Johnstown Flood.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-86) When word of the dam's failure was telegraphed to Pittsburgh, Frick and other members of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club gathered to form the Pittsburgh Relief Committee for assistance to the flood victims as well as determining never to speak publicly about the club or the flood. This strategy was a success, and Knox and Reed were able to fend off all lawsuits that would have placed blame upon the club's members. Although Cambria Iron and Steel's facilities were heavily damaged by the flood, they returned to full production within a year. After the flood, Carnegie built Johnstown a new library to replace the one built by Cambria's chief legal counsel Cyrus Elder, which was destroyed in the flood. The Carnegie-donated library is now owned by the Johnstown Area Heritage Association and houses the Flood Museum. ### 1892: Homestead Strike [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Homestead_Strike_-_Mob_attacking_Pinkerton_men.jpg/500px-Homestead_Strike_-_Mob_attacking_Pinkerton_men.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homestead_Strike_-_Mob_attacking_Pinkerton_men.jpg) The Homestead Strike Main article: [Homestead Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Strike "Homestead Strike") The [Homestead Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Strike "Homestead Strike") was a bloody labor confrontation lasting 143 days in 1892, one of the most serious in U.S. history. The conflict was centered on Carnegie Steel's main plant in [Homestead, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead,_Pennsylvania "Homestead, Pennsylvania") , and grew out of a labor dispute between the [Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalgamated_Association_of_Iron_and_Steel_Workers "Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers") (AA) and the [Carnegie Steel Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company") . Carnegie left on a trip to Scotland before the unrest peaked.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Carnegie,_Andrew_1920-87) In doing so, Carnegie left mediation of the dispute in the hands of his associate and partner [Henry Clay Frick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Clay_Frick "Henry Clay Frick") . Frick was well known in industrial circles for maintaining staunch anti-union sentiment. With the collective bargaining agreement between the union and company expiring at the end of June, Frick and the leaders of the local AA union entered into negotiations in February. With the steel industry doing well and prices higher, the AA asked for a wage increase; the AA represented about 800 of the 3,800 workers at the plant. Frick immediately countered with an average 22% wage decrease that would affect nearly half the union's membership and remove a number of positions from the bargaining unit.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-88) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Frick_to_Carnegie_letter_about_the_arming_of_the_Pinkertons.jpg/960px-Frick_to_Carnegie_letter_about_the_arming_of_the_Pinkertons.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frick_to_Carnegie_letter_about_the_arming_of_the_Pinkertons.jpg) Frick's letter to Carnegie describing the plans and munitions that will be on the barges when the Pinkertons arrive to confront the strikers in Homestead The union and company failed to come to an agreement, and management locked the union out. Workers considered the stoppage a "[lockout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockout_(industry) "Lockout (industry)") " by management and not a "strike" by workers. As such, the workers would have been well within their rights to protest, and subsequent government action would have been a set of criminal procedures designed to crush what was seen as a pivotal demonstration of the growing [labor rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_history_of_the_United_States "Labor history of the United States") , strongly opposed by management. Frick brought in thousands of strikebreakers to work the steel mills and [Pinkerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinkerton_National_Detective_Agency "Pinkerton National Detective Agency") agents to safeguard them. On July 6, the arrival of a force of 300 Pinkerton agents from New York City and Chicago, Illinois, resulted in a fight in which 10 men—seven strikers and three Pinkertons—were killed and hundreds were injured. Pennsylvania Governor [Robert Pattison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Pattison "Robert E. Pattison") ordered two brigades of the state militia to the strike site. Then allegedly in response to the fight between the striking workers and the Pinkertons, [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism") [Alexander Berkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Berkman "Alexander Berkman") shot at Frick in an attempted assassination, wounding him. While not directly connected to the strike, Berkman was tied in for the assassination attempt. According to Berkman, "... with the elimination of Frick, responsibility for Homestead conditions would rest with Carnegie."[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-89) Afterwards, the company successfully resumed operations with non-union immigrant employees in place of the Homestead plant workers, and Carnegie returned to the United States.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-Carnegie,_Andrew_1920-87) However, Carnegie's reputation was permanently damaged by the Homestead events. ### Theodore Roosevelt According to David Nasaw, after 1898, when the United States entered a war with Spain, Carnegie increasingly devoted his energy to supporting pacifism. He strongly opposed the war and the subsequent imperialistic American takeover of the Philippines. When [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") became president in 1901, Carnegie and Roosevelt were in frequent contact. They exchanged letters, communicated through mutual friends such as Secretary of State [John Hay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hay "John Hay") , and met in person. Carnegie hoped that Roosevelt would turn the Philippines free. He saluted Roosevelt for forcing Germany and Britain to arbitrate their conflict with Venezuela in 1903, and especially for becoming the mediator who negotiated an end to the war between Russia and Japan in 1907–1908. Roosevelt relied on Carnegie for financing his expedition to [Africa in 1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian%E2%80%93Roosevelt_African_Expedition "Smithsonian–Roosevelt African Expedition") . In return he asked the ex-president to mediate the growing conflict between the cousins who ruled Britain and Germany. Roosevelt started to do so but the scheme collapsed when king [Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VII "Edward VII") suddenly died.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-90) [\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-91) Nasaw argues that Roosevelt systematically deceived and manipulated Carnegie and held the elderly man in contempt. Nasaw quotes a private letter Roosevelt wrote to [Whitelaw Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitelaw_Reid "Whitelaw Reid") in 1905:[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie#cite_note-92) > \[I have\] tried hard to like Carnegie, but it is pretty difficult. There is no type of man for whom I feel a more contemptuous abhorrence than for the one who makes a God of mere money-making and at the same time is always yelling out that kind of utterly stupid condemnation of war which in almost every case springs from a combination of defective physical courage, of unmanly shrinking from pain and effort, and of hopelessly twisted ideals. All the suffering from Spanish war comes far short of the suffering, preventable and non-preventable, among the operators of the Carnegie steel works, and among the small investors, during the time that Carnegie was making his fortune…. It is as noxious folly to denounce war per se as it is to denounce business per se. Unrighteous war is a hideous evil; but I am not at all sure that it is worse evil than business unrighteousness.
